why: Detect a cycle in a directed graph with DFS three-colour marking: a node is white (unseen), grey (on the current DFS path) or black (finished). Reaching a grey node means an edge points back into the current path, which is a cycle.
hints: In an undirected graph, meeting any visited node hints at a cycle. Why is that not enough when edges have a direction? Think of two paths that merge at the same node.
Only an edge back to a node that is still on the current DFS path closes a cycle. Keep three states: unvisited, on the path, finished.
Run DFS from every unvisited node with an explicit stack of (node, next-edge index). Mark grey on entry and black on exit; an edge to a grey node returns true. O(n + edges).
pitfalls: A self-loop [v, v] is a cycle; the grey check catches it because v is grey when its own edge is scanned.
Recursive DFS overflows at 10^5 nodes in Python; use an explicit stack.
Two paths that meet at a finished (black) node are not a cycle (example 2).
